record.title: SpecGuard uses Lean certificates to detect task–test conflicts before coding agents run
record.summary: Biyani and Dvijotham introduce SpecGuard, a pre-execution verifier for coding tasks whose natural-language intent may conflict with their tests. Separate agents formalize the task description/codebase and the test requirements, and a Lean kernel checks whether the generated representations can both be satisfied; the result may be conflict, no-conflict or inconclusive. In the authors’ mutated SWE-bench evaluation, GPT-5.6 Sol formally certified 51.1% of conflicts, while its conflict-miss rate was 8.1% versus 39.8% for an LLM-judge baseline. On 22 selected naturally occurring GitHub conflicts, the CLI returned nine conflict verdicts, eight with Lean certificates. These are author-reported preprint results. The kernel proves inconsistency between generated formal representations; semantic fidelity to the original task remains a separate and material limitation.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: Biyani and Dvijotham published the SpecGuard preprint, arXiv:2610.09159v1, on 2026-10-06.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On mutated SWE-bench tasks, the authors report that GPT-5.6 Sol produced Lean conflict certificates for 51.1% of conflicts; its conflict-miss rate was 8.1%, compared with 39.8% for an LLM-judge baseline. The authors report a 6.0% false-positive rate for SpecGuard and 2.3% for the judge on corresponding unmutated tasks.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On a selected set of 22 naturally occurring GitHub test conflicts, the authors report nine CLI conflict verdicts, eight with Lean certificates and one with execution-only evidence; the remaining outcomes were twelve inconclusive and one no-conflict.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors state that a Lean certificate proves inconsistency between the generated task specification and formalized tests; it does not by itself establish that either formalization faithfully represents the original task.

evidence_gaps.description: The arXiv paper links a GitHub repository, but the URL returned 404 in this activation; code and pinned revisions could not be inspected.
No independent reproduction of the three-run GPT-5.6 Sol comparison, model-specific rates, cost or natural-conflict CLI evaluation was established.

A certificate proves a contradiction between generated formalizations, but semantic correspondence to the original task remains a separate assumption; six of 60 manually reviewed formalizations were spurious and two weak.

Evaluation is limited to coding tasks with value-semantics behavior and a trusted task description; coverage of side effects, concurrency, external dependencies and adversarial task descriptions is unknown.

brief.importance_rationale: If the bounded results reproduce, a pre-execution check that can produce independently kernel-checkable certificates of conflicts between trusted task intent and untrusted tests could materially change how coding-agent pipelines gate impossible or adversarial work. Evidence is a single preprint with substantial semantic-fidelity, false-positive and task-scope limits.
limitations: A kernel-checked proof establishes inconsistency between generated representations, not that the specification or test transcription faithfully captures the source task.
The authors' manual audit found 52 of 60 reviewed formalizations faithful, six spurious and two weak; in an audit of incorrect verdicts, connector alignment was the most common failure source.

On corresponding unmutated tasks, SpecGuard's reported false-positive rate was 6.0%, higher than the LLM judge's 2.3%; treating inconclusive outcomes as blocked increases coverage but withholds some unmodified tasks.
The method targets behavior expressible as executable value semantics and assumes the task description is trusted; adversarial modification of the description is outside its threat model.
The 22 natural conflicts were selected from GitHub issues/PRs and are not a prevalence sample; nine received conflict verdicts and twelve were inconclusive.
The paper-linked GitHub repository returned 404 in this activation. Reported results have not been independently reproduced.
brief.summary: Biyani and Dvijotham introduce SpecGuard, a pre-execution verifier for coding tasks whose natural-language intent may conflict with their tests. Separate agents formalize the task description/codebase and the test requirements, and a Lean kernel checks whether the generated representations can both be satisfied; the result may be conflict, no-conflict or inconclusive. In the authors’ mutated SWE-bench evaluation, GPT-5.6 Sol formally certified 51.1% of conflicts, while its conflict-miss rate was 8.1% versus 39.8% for an LLM-judge baseline. On 22 selected naturally occurring GitHub conflicts, the CLI returned nine conflict verdicts, eight with Lean certificates. These are author-reported preprint results. technical.claimed_result: Authors report 51.1% Lean-certified conflicts with GPT-5.6 Sol, an 8.1% conflict-miss rate versus 39.8% for the LLM judge, and eight Lean certificates among nine conflict verdicts on a selected set of 22 natural cases.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper reports average cost per task of $0.26 for SpecGuard with GPT-5.6 Sol ($0.46 with paired tests) and $0.84 for the five-vote LLM judge; these are author-reported task costs, not full deployment or maintenance economics.
technical.demonstrated_result: The arXiv preprint and its reported method/results are public. The linked code URL returned 404; no code execution or independent reproduction was performed.
technical.implementation_status: The paper describes a standalone CLI and states that source code accompanies the submission, but its linked GitHub URL returned 404 in this activation; artifact availability is unresolved.
technical.mechanism: A SpecAgent derives a Lean executable specification from task description and codebase without seeing tests; a separate TestAgent formalizes test demands; a Certifier connects the representations and asks Lean to check joint satisfiability. Outputs are conflict, no-conflict or inconclusive. A certificate proves conflict only between the generated representations.
technical.regime: Coding tasks whose intended behavior can be represented through executable value semantics; task descriptions are trusted, while tests and codebase may be corrupted or adversarial. Evaluations use mutated SWE-bench/LiveCodeBench tasks and 22 selected natural GitHub conflicts.
technical.reproducibility: The authors provide experimental details and say code is included, but the linked repository was unavailable at review time. No independent reproduction was established. Manual audit found 52/60 reviewed formalizations faithful, 6 spurious and 2 weak.
technical.strongest_baseline: An LLM-judge majority vote over five judgments, plus a Python reference-model baseline; the latter receives paired original and corrupted tests, unlike the main SpecGuard comparison.

brief.title: SpecGuard uses Lean certificates to detect task–test conflicts before coding agents run
brief.why_it_matters: If reproduced, a pre-execution check that surfaces impossible or adversarial task/test combinations with an independently checkable certificate could prevent some coding agents from being rewarded for test gaming before they act. The method explicitly separates a model's interpretation from the kernel's proof and allows inconclusive outcomes. Its usefulness depends on faithful translation of task intent and tests, and the current evaluation is limited to selected coding-task settings.
